note: Tier D is refused from every package, first-party included. v3 does not schematise Tier D parameters, and carries no vector exercising one — but the refusals themselves are required. A rule with no vector is a rule an implementation can omit and still claim conformance.
refusal_note: `error` is the class a conforming loader raises. A Tier D declaration is a validation error, not a security error, and the same one from every package: v2 raised a security error for community packages because provenance decided who held the authority. In v3 nobody holds it, so provenance is not the question. `must_name` lists identifiers the message must contain.

cases.name: trigger_declaring_tier_d_refused
cases.why: Tier D fires before any LLM and cannot be overridden. It is the one tier that removes the operator rather than adding one.

cases.name: first_party_trigger_declaring_tier_d_refused
cases.why: The `bundled` sentinel does not buy Tier D. v2 accepted it from packages shipping with the runtime; that was containment, not ownership, and left the safety envelope a property of which skills are installed.

cases.name: tier_d_action_in_available_refused
cases.why: Tier D is not reachable from a package by declaration.

cases.name: tier_d_action_reached_by_escalation_refused
cases.registry_premise: The runtime registry gives `emergency_cutoff` a minimum tier of D.
cases.why: A package declaring a Tier D action below its minimum, to get it into a default list. This is the only shape in which a Tier D action can reach a default list at all, so it is the case that tests the escalation cap: Tier D is not reachable from a package by escalation any more than by declaration.
cases.note: The registry is runtime-owned and outside this contract, so the premise is stated rather than assumed. A consumer whose registry does not know `emergency_cutoff` cannot run this case and should say so rather than pass it.

cases.name: default_action_not_declared_in_available_refused
cases.why: A v3 invariant in its own right, and the rule that makes the Tier D default-list case untestable in isolation — so it is covered deliberately here rather than incidentally there. `log_to_dashboard` is a Tier A action, so nothing about Tier D is involved.

cases.name: bypass_llm_refused_on_any_trigger
cases.why: `bypass_llm` is the Tier D execution property. A package reaching it under another tier would have Tier D behaviour without the label.

cases.name: escalation_to_tier_c_accepted
cases.why: A package may raise an action's tier to at most C. The cap is what makes the Tier D prohibition meaningful rather than cosmetic.

isolation_note: Each manifest is valid in every respect except the one the case names. A vector carrying a second defect lets a conforming implementation refuse for that instead and never reach the boundary under test, which reports coverage that does not exist.
tier_d_in_defaults_note: The contract's Vectors section asks for a package whose trigger default actions include a Tier D action. No manifest makes that the only defect: an action absent from `actions.available` is refused as an undeclared default, one declared at `D` is refused by the Tier D declaration rule, and one declared below `D` is refused by the minimum-tier rule. The three cases here cover those paths separately rather than one vector that could be refused for any of them.
